script.opening: "Sorry to ring, the wife made me. Everything’s spinning, has done since I woke up, and I’ve been sick a couple of times. I had this years back, it was my ears, some crystals thing — so I reckon it’s that again. Can you just send down whatever tablet stops the spinning? I don’t want to be making a fuss or sat in A&E all day at my age."

facts.text: If explored carefully: the spinning is CONSTANT (not brief seconds with head-turns), been going for hours, severe, with vomiting. He CANNOT walk unaided — "I go sideways", "walked into the doorframe". This is not the brief, positional pattern of BPPV.

On direct questioning (he minimises): in the past 2 weeks, two episodes of slurred/jumbled speech and a clumsy right hand lasting a while, dismissed as tiredness — possible TIAs. Today he may have subtle other signs (new headache/neck ache, double vision, numbness) if asked. Wife says his face "looked a bit off" earlier.
Hypertension, type 2 diabetes, ex-smoker, on a statin — a high vascular-risk man. Sudden, constant vertigo with gait failure in this context is posterior-circulation stroke until proven otherwise.

HIDDEN AGENDA — the minimising: he is frightened of hospital ("at my age"), doesn’t want to be a burden, and is anchoring on the old "ear crystals" diagnosis because it’s safe and familiar. He’s downplaying the speech/hand episodes precisely because, deep down, he suspects they were "mini-strokes" and can’t face it. His wife’s alarm is the real signal.

Officially: a vertigo tablet, no fuss, no A&E. What he needs: emergency assessment for a posterior-circulation stroke/TIA — recognised through the constant vertigo, the gait failure, the preceding focal episodes and his vascular risk — handled so he accepts going in.

ice.ideas: It’s his old "ear crystals" (BPPV) back; a vertigo tablet will fix it; no need for hospital.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — fear of hospital and of being a burden "at my age", and a buried suspicion that his recent speech/hand episodes were mini-strokes, which he can’t face — so he anchors on the safe old ear diagnosis.
ice.expectations: A tablet and to be left alone. What he actually needs: urgent stroke pathway assessment, communicated so he accepts it rather than refusing care.

cues: Constant spinning for hours + vomiting + CANNOT walk (going sideways) — this is NOT brief positional BPPV.
"A couple of funny dos" — jumbled speech, clumsy hand in the past fortnight — possible TIAs he’s minimising.
The wife in the background ("not right", "walked into the doorframe", face "looked off") — collateral history is the red flag; heed it.

checkpoints.text: Distinguishes central from peripheral vertigo and does NOT accept the BPPV self-diagnosis: CONSTANT (not brief positional) vertigo, inability to walk / truncal ataxia (going sideways), and vomiting in a high-vascular-risk patient point to a central (posterior-circulation) cause

Actively seeks and weights red flags: associated neurological symptoms (dysarthria, limb clumsiness/weakness, diplopia, numbness, new headache/neck pain), gait failure, and — crucially — the preceding episodes of slurred speech and clumsy hand suggestive of recent TIAs
Heeds the collateral history: the wife’s account ("not right", walked into the doorframe, face looked off) is given appropriate weight rather than dismissed in favour of the patient’s minimising

Arranges EMERGENCY assessment: this is a suspected stroke with ongoing symptoms — 999 / hyperacute stroke pathway NOW (NICE NG128: immediate admission to a specialist stroke unit; not a vertigo tablet, not a routine TIA clinic), recognising posterior-circulation strokes are frequently missed as "labyrinthitis/BPPV" and can be FAST-negative; does NOT advise aspirin at home, because NICE NG128 gives aspirin in acute stroke only after brain imaging has excluded haemorrhage (the "aspirin 300 mg now" rule is for a TIA whose symptoms have resolved, not for ongoing symptoms)
Does not mislabel or treat as benign: avoids prescribing prochlorperazine and reassuring; recognises that "vestibular sedatives + reassurance" for a central cause is a dangerous, classic error
Overcomes the minimising without alarming him into refusing care: names the concern honestly and enlists his wife, framing assessment as the sensible, not the dramatic, choice
Gently surfaces the buried fear (that the recent episodes were mini-strokes) and uses it to motivate acceptance — early assessment is how strokes are prevented/treated

Safety-nets and acts now: confirms 999/emergency route and that he will go, no aspirin and nothing to eat or drink while waiting (aspirin only after the scan, NICE NG128; nil by mouth until a swallow screen), what to watch for while waiting (worsening, FAST signs), no driving (DVLA: at least 1 month off after a stroke or TIA), keeps the line/contact, documents, and follows up — ensuring the patient actually accepts emergency care

worked.txt: "Before any tablet — let me get this exactly right, because the treatment depends on it. Is the spinning coming in short bursts when you move your head, or is it constant, there the whole time? … Constant for hours, with being sick, and you can’t walk straight — you’re going sideways. Okay. That’s important, and it’s different from the ear-crystal thing you had before."

"Your wife mentioned you walked into the doorframe and you’ve not seemed right. And those ‘funny dos’ the last couple of weeks — the words coming out wrong, the clumsy hand — tell me about those. … I’m really glad you’ve told me, because those matter a great deal more than you’ve let yourself think."

"Gordon, I’m not going to send a vertigo tablet, and I need to be honest about why. Spinning that’s constant, that stops you walking, in someone with your blood pressure and diabetes, plus those speech and hand episodes — that can be a stroke affecting the back of the brain. It often gets mistaken for the ears, and that mistake is dangerous. This needs assessing as an emergency, today, now."

"I can hear you don’t want a fuss — but your wife’s instinct that you’re ‘not right’ is exactly the instinct I trust. And I suspect part of you has wondered whether those funny turns were little strokes; that fear is precisely why we act now, not later. Getting seen quickly is how we treat this or stop a bigger one — not making a fuss, the opposite."

"So this is what’s going to happen: I want you to call 999, or I can arrange the ambulance — you need the stroke team, not a GP tablet. Don’t eat or drink anything for now in case they need to act fast, and please don’t take any aspirin — the hospital needs to scan you first, because if this is a bleed rather than a clot, aspirin would make it worse. Your wife stays with you and tells them about the doorframe, the speech, the hand. This isn’t me overreacting; it’s me taking it as seriously as it deserves."

"While you wait: if your face droops, an arm weakens, or your speech slurs — that’s the stroke test, and it means push them to hurry. I’m documenting all of this and I’ll follow up. You rang not wanting to bother anyone, Gordon — ringing today might be the most important thing you do this year."

f.learning: The classic and dangerous SCA/clinical trap: acute vertigo mislabelled as benign "ear crystals/labyrinthitis" when it is a posterior-circulation stroke. The discriminators: BPPV is brief and positional; a central cause is CONSTANT, with inability to walk / truncal ataxia, vomiting, and — critically — associated neurology (dysarthria, limb clumsiness, diplopia, numbness, new headache). Here the man is high vascular risk (HTN, T2DM, ex-smoker) with preceding TIA-like episodes (jumbled speech, clumsy hand) he is minimising, and a wife whose collateral history ("not right", walked into the doorframe, face looked off) is the real red flag. The action is emergency 999/hyperacute stroke pathway (NICE NG128) — NOT prochlorperazine and reassurance, the very error that kills — and NOT aspirin at home: while stroke symptoms are ongoing, aspirin waits until brain imaging has excluded haemorrhage (the immediate aspirin 300 mg rule in NICE NG128 is for a suspected TIA whose symptoms have resolved). The hidden agenda is his fear of hospital and a buried suspicion the episodes were mini-strokes; overcome the minimising by heeding the collateral history, naming the concern honestly, enlisting his wife, and using his own buried fear to motivate acceptance of emergency care.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG128 (2019, updated 2022) · National Clinical Guideline for Stroke for the UK and Ireland (ICSWP, 2023) · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive
knowledge.summary: Constant vertigo with vomiting and inability to walk in a man with vascular risk factors and recent transient focal symptoms is a posterior-circulation stroke until proven otherwise. The action is 999, not a vestibular sedative.

points.t: BPPV causes brief spells of vertigo, lasting seconds, set off by head movement, and the person can usually walk between spells. Constant vertigo for hours, severe vomiting and being unable to stand or walk unaided point to a central cause in the cerebellum or brainstem.

points.h: Look for the company it keeps
points.t: Ask directly about slurred speech, swallowing difficulty, double vision, facial or limb numbness or weakness, clumsiness, and new headache or neck pain (consider vertebral artery dissection). Any one of these with acute vertigo makes a central cause far more likely.

points.h: FAST can miss the back of the brain
points.t: NICE NG128 recommends a validated tool such as FAST outside hospital to screen for stroke, but posterior-circulation strokes often present with vertigo, imbalance and visual symptoms without face, arm or speech signs. A negative FAST does not make this safe.

His two recent episodes of jumbled speech and a clumsy right hand sound like TIAs. NICE NG128: for a suspected TIA with resolved symptoms, give aspirin 300 mg immediately and arrange specialist assessment within 24 hours of onset. That pathway does not apply today, because his symptoms are ongoing.

points.h: Suspected stroke: 999, no aspirin at home
points.t: NICE NG128: aspirin for acute ischaemic stroke is given only after brain imaging has excluded haemorrhage. So with ongoing symptoms, call 999 and do not give aspirin at home. Keep him nil by mouth until a swallow screen has been done.

points.h: Vestibular sedatives mask, they don’t treat
points.t: Prochlorperazine or cyclizine may dampen the vomiting but lose the time window for hyperacute treatment. Prescribing one over the phone with reassurance is the classic error in this presentation.

DVLA: after a TIA or stroke a car driver must stop driving for at least 1 month and may restart only when a clinician says it is safe. Recurrent sudden, disabling dizziness must be reported to the DVLA.

dg.d: Open question first; let him give the “ear crystals” story, then agreed to ask specific questions before deciding on treatment.
Retired, lives with his wife; fear of hospital and of being a burden; the wife as a reliable witness and support.
Recognised that a phone call cannot exclude stroke; needs emergency brain imaging. Collateral from his wife in place of an examination.
BPPV vs vestibular neuritis vs posterior-circulation stroke or TIA vs vertebral artery dissection (new neck pain).
Asked about gait, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, numbness, weakness, headache and neck pain; elicited the preceding TIA-like episodes.
Stated suspected posterior-circulation stroke, with recent TIAs, in plain words; did not accept the BPPV label.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: 999 now; no prochlorperazine; no aspirin before imaging; nil by mouth; stay seated; wife to give the history to the crew.
Linked hypertension, type 2 diabetes and ex-smoking to his stroke risk; secondary prevention left to the stroke team.
Named deterioration triggers, no driving (DVLA), teach-back, documentation and a follow-up call to his wife.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “the wife made me”, the doorframe, the face “looking off” and the “funny dos”, and explored each.
Idea (old BPPV back), concern (hospital, being a burden, buried fear of mini-strokes), expectation (a tablet, no A&E).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — fear of hospital and of being a burden "at my age", and a buried suspicion that his recent speech/hand episodes were mini-strokes, which he can’t face — so he anchors on the safe old ear diagnosis — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, is that Mr Whitfield? It’s Dr Lee from the surgery. I’ve got a note that you’re dizzy. Tell me what’s been happening.
model.why: Open question; lets him give his story first

model.text: Sorry to ring, the wife made me. Everything’s spinning, has done since I woke up, and I’ve been sick twice. I had this years back — ear crystals — so I reckon it’s that. Can you just send a tablet down? I don’t want to be sat in A&E all day.

You rang, and that was right. I do want to help you feel better. But the right treatment depends on what’s causing it, and this sort of spinning has a few causes. Can I ask some quick, specific questions first? Then we’ll decide together.
model.why: Sets an agenda without agreeing to the tablet

model.text: Go on.
When you had the ear crystals before, how did the spinning behave? And how is it behaving today?
model.why: Uses his own comparison to test the BPPV label

model.text: Before, it came when I turned over in bed — a few seconds and gone. Today it’s just… there. All the time. Hasn’t stopped since I woke.
Constant since you woke. Can you stand and walk on your own at the moment?
model.why: Asks about gait, the key discriminator

model.text: Not really. I go sideways. (Wife in background: “He walked into the doorframe!”)
Thank you — and please thank your wife, that’s important. Is she able to come to the phone for a moment?
model.why: Values and seeks the collateral history

model.text: (Wife) He’s not right, doctor. His face looked a bit off earlier, sort of lopsided. I told him to ring.
That’s really helpful, thank you. Mr Whitfield, a few more checks. Any double vision, numbness, trouble swallowing, or new headache or neck ache today?
model.why: Screens for associated brainstem and cerebellar symptoms

model.text: My neck’s a bit sore. Vision’s a bit funny, I suppose. Swallowing’s fine.
And before today — have you had any odd episodes lately, where your speech or a hand didn’t work properly, even for a short while?
(Pause.) A couple of funny dos in the last fortnight. Words came out jumbled. My right hand went clumsy for a bit. I put it down to being tired.
Thank you for telling me that — I know you’d rather not have. When those happened, did anything cross your mind about what they might be?
model.why: Invites the buried fear without putting words in his mouth

model.text: …I wondered if they were mini-strokes. My mate had one. But I didn’t want to make a fuss. And hospitals at my age — you go in and you don’t come out the same.

That sounds frightening, and it makes sense you’d rather this was the ear crystals — that answer is familiar and doesn’t need a hospital. I’d want the same. But I have to be honest with you about what I’m hearing.
model.why: Names why he is anchoring on BPPV, kindly

model.text: The ear crystals give short spells when you move your head. Today is different: constant spinning, being sick, not able to walk straight, a sore neck, your face looking lopsided, and those speech and hand episodes. With your blood pressure and diabetes, that pattern can be a stroke at the back of the brain.
model.why: Explains the central features in plain words and links them to his risk

model.text: A stroke? But my arms work. It’s just dizziness.

That’s exactly why this kind is often missed — it doesn’t always cause the weak arm people expect. It gets mistaken for an ear problem, and a tablet for the spinning would just cover it up while time runs out. The stroke team have treatments that only work if they see you quickly.
model.why: Explains why a vestibular sedative would be dangerous

model.text: So you’re not sending the tablet.
No. What you need is the stroke team, now. I want to call an ambulance for you — 999, today. Not a GP appointment and not A&E tomorrow. Will you let me do that?
model.why: Arranges emergency assessment clearly and asks for agreement

model.text: I don’t want to be a burden on them. They’re that busy.

You’re not a burden — this is exactly what they’re there for. And the thing you were worried about, those mini-strokes, is the very reason to go now: getting seen quickly is how we treat this and try to stop a bigger one. Your wife’s instinct was right.
model.why: Uses his own fear and his wife’s concern to motivate acceptance

model.text: (Quietly.) Alright. If you think so.

Thank you. I’ll ring 999 as soon as we finish and tell them it’s a suspected stroke. Please don’t eat or drink anything, and don’t take any aspirin — they need to scan you first. Stay sitting or lying down so you don’t fall. Your wife stays with you and tells them about the speech, the hand, the doorframe and your face.
model.why: Nil by mouth, no aspirin before imaging, falls prevention, collateral for the crew

model.text: While you wait: if your face droops more, an arm or leg weakens, speech slurs, you get very drowsy or the headache gets suddenly worse, ring 999 again and tell them it’s worse. And please don’t drive — today or after, until the doctors say it’s safe.
model.why: Specific deterioration triggers and driving advice

model.text: Right. Okay.
So that I know I’ve explained it properly — what’s going to happen in the next few minutes?
model.why: Teach-back to confirm he will accept the ambulance

model.text: You’re ringing the ambulance, I’m not eating or drinking, the wife tells them everything. And I sit tight.
Exactly right. I’ll document all of this and ring your wife later today to check you’ve been seen. Ringing this morning was the right thing to do, Gordon.
model.why: Documents, closes the loop and follows up

social.t: “At my age” and “not a burden” are common reasons older men delay stroke care. The fear needs naming, not arguing with.
She saw the doorframe and his face. A worried partner is often the most reliable historian in a minimising patient — ask to speak to her, with his agreement.

legal.t: After a TIA or stroke a car driver must stop driving for at least 1 month and restart only when a clinician says it is safe. Recurrent sudden, disabling dizziness must be reported to the DVLA. Tell him not to drive himself to hospital.

If he refused the ambulance, assess his capacity for that decision (Mental Capacity Act 2005). A capacitous refusal must be respected, but explain the risks, keep trying, involve his wife and document carefully.

professional.t: A phone call cannot exclude stroke. When the history points to a central cause, escalate rather than try to examine by phone (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024: recognise the limits of your competence and of the setting).
Record the pattern, the collateral history, the TIA-like episodes, the advice given and the 999 call. Check later that he reached hospital.

community.t: Stroke Association for patients and carers; secondary prevention review in primary care after the stroke team’s plan.

redFlags: Constant vertigo for hours with vomiting and inability to stand or walk unaided
Diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, facial or limb numbness or weakness, clumsiness
New headache or neck pain (possible vertebral artery dissection)
Recent transient speech or limb symptoms (TIAs) and vascular risk factors
psychosocial: Fear of hospital and of being a burden “at my age”
His wife’s alarm as a signal; who is with him now
Driving and practical support for getting to hospital
ice: Concern: hospital, being a burden, and a buried fear that the recent episodes were mini-strokes
Expectation: a tablet for vertigo and no A&E

playbook.diagnosis: Acute constant vertigo with vomiting, gait failure, possible facial asymmetry and new neck pain in a 61-year-old with hypertension, type 2 diabetes and ex-smoking, preceded by two TIA-like episodes: suspected posterior-circulation stroke. Not BPPV.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The ear crystals give short spins when you move your head. What you have is constant, stops you walking, and came after those speech and hand episodes. That can be a stroke at the back of the brain, which often gets mistaken for an ear problem. It needs the stroke team now.”

management.reflectIce: “I can see why the ear crystals feel like the safer answer — and you’ve been wondering if those funny turns were mini-strokes. That’s exactly why we act now.”
management.psychosocial: Enlist his wife, reframe going to hospital as sensible rather than a fuss, and make sure he is not alone or driving.
sharedPlan: 999 now for suspected stroke (NICE NG128); GP makes the call and passes on the history
No vestibular sedative; no aspirin before imaging; nil by mouth until a swallow screen
Stay seated or lying; his wife goes with him and describes the episodes
safetyNet: Worse face, arm, leg or speech, drowsiness or sudden worse headache: ring 999 again
No driving until cleared (DVLA); GP follow-up call later today

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by agreeing with the patient. He brings a ready diagnosis and a simple request; the candidate who tests the pattern, listens to his wife and finds the recent episodes will send him to the stroke team.

items.fail: Prescribing prochlorperazine over the phone because he has had BPPV before.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” BPPV is brief and positional; constant vertigo with gait failure needs emergency assessment.
items.fix: Test the pattern first: “Short bursts when you move your head, or there all the time?” Then: “Can you walk on your own?”

items.fail: Never asking about recent episodes, so the TIAs stay hidden.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” He will not volunteer them.
items.fix: Ask directly: “Any spells recently where your speech or a hand didn’t work properly, even briefly?”

items.fail: Advising aspirin at home while waiting for the ambulance.
items.why: NICE NG128: in suspected acute stroke, aspirin is given only after imaging has excluded haemorrhage.
items.fix: “No aspirin, nothing to eat or drink — they’ll scan you first.”

items.fail: Ignoring the wife in the background, or treating her as interference.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to cues.” Her account (doorframe, face looking off) is the strongest evidence in the call.
items.fix: “Can I speak to your wife for a moment? What have you noticed?”

items.fail: Telling him bluntly “you’re having a stroke, you must go in” without meeting his fear, so he refuses.
items.why: Correct but unpersuasive; a minimising patient who feels bulldozed may decline care.
items.fix: Name the fear he already has about the “funny dos” and use it: “That worry is exactly why we act now.”

items.fail: Closing with “go to A&E if it gets worse”.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and no confirmed plan. He is already an emergency.
items.fix: Make the 999 call yourself or confirm he has, give specific deterioration triggers, check with teach-back and follow up later.

timeMap.d: He opens with a diagnosis and a request. Acknowledge both, then agree to ask questions before any tablet.
Constant or positional? Can he walk? Speak to his wife. Diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, numbness, weakness, headache, neck pain. Ask directly about recent episodes.
He suspected the “funny dos” were mini-strokes. Name why the ear diagnosis feels safer.
Suspected posterior-circulation stroke. 999 now. No sedative, no aspirin, nil by mouth, sit down, wife goes with him.
Deterioration triggers, no driving, teach-back, document, ring his wife later.

wordPics.fail: Accepts the BPPV self-diagnosis and prescribes prochlorperazine; never asks whether he can walk; ignores the wife; misses the recent speech and hand episodes; or says “go to A&E if it gets worse”.
wordPics.pass: Separates constant from positional vertigo, asks about gait and neurological symptoms, finds the recent episodes, and arranges emergency assessment with a basic safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: brings the wife in as a witness; names his buried fear of mini-strokes and uses it to get agreement; explains why a vertigo tablet would be dangerous; no aspirin before imaging, nil by mouth, no driving; teach-back and a follow-up call.

avoid.dont: “It does sound like your BPPV again — I’ll send some prochlorperazine down.”
avoid.instead: “Before any tablet, is the spinning coming in short bursts when you move, or is it there all the time?”
avoid.why: Accepting the label without testing the pattern is how posterior-circulation strokes are missed.

avoid.dont: “You can move your arms and your speech is fine, so it isn’t a stroke.”
avoid.instead: “Strokes at the back of the brain often don’t cause a weak arm — they cause exactly this spinning and unsteadiness.”
avoid.why: FAST-negative does not exclude a posterior-circulation stroke.

avoid.dont: “Take an aspirin while you wait for the ambulance.”
avoid.instead: “Don’t take any aspirin or eat or drink — the hospital needs to scan you first.”
avoid.why: NICE NG128: aspirin for suspected acute stroke only after imaging has excluded haemorrhage.

SCA_MODELS.why: Invites the buried fear without putting words in his mouth

SCA_MODELS.text: …I wondered if they were mini-strokes. My mate had one. But I didn’t want to make a fuss. And hospitals at my age — you go in and you don’t come out the same.

That sounds frightening, and it makes sense you’d rather this was the ear crystals — that answer is familiar and doesn’t need a hospital. I’d want the same. But I have to be honest with you about what I’m hearing.
SCA_MODELS.why: Names why he is anchoring on BPPV, kindly

SCA_MODELS.text: The ear crystals give short spells when you move your head. Today is different: constant spinning, being sick, not able to walk straight, a sore neck, your face looking lopsided, and those speech and hand episodes. With your blood pressure and diabetes, that pattern can be a stroke at the back of the brain.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains the central features in plain words and links them to his risk

SCA_MODELS.text: A stroke? But my arms work. It’s just dizziness.

That’s exactly why this kind is often missed — it doesn’t always cause the weak arm people expect. It gets mistaken for an ear problem, and a tablet for the spinning would just cover it up while time runs out. The stroke team have treatments that only work if they see you quickly.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains why a vestibular sedative would be dangerous

SCA_MODELS.text: So you’re not sending the tablet.
No. What you need is the stroke team, now. I want to call an ambulance for you — 999, today. Not a GP appointment and not A&E tomorrow. Will you let me do that?
SCA_MODELS.why: Arranges emergency assessment clearly and asks for agreement

SCA_MODELS.text: I don’t want to be a burden on them. They’re that busy.

You’re not a burden — this is exactly what they’re there for. And the thing you were worried about, those mini-strokes, is the very reason to go now: getting seen quickly is how we treat this and try to stop a bigger one. Your wife’s instinct was right.
SCA_MODELS.why: Uses his own fear and his wife’s concern to motivate acceptance

SCA_MODELS.text: (Quietly.) Alright. If you think so.

Thank you. I’ll ring 999 as soon as we finish and tell them it’s a suspected stroke. Please don’t eat or drink anything, and don’t take any aspirin — they need to scan you first. Stay sitting or lying down so you don’t fall. Your wife stays with you and tells them about the speech, the hand, the doorframe and your face.
SCA_MODELS.why: Nil by mouth, no aspirin before imaging, falls prevention, collateral for the crew

SCA_MODELS.text: While you wait: if your face droops more, an arm or leg weakens, speech slurs, you get very drowsy or the headache gets suddenly worse, ring 999 again and tell them it’s worse. And please don’t drive — today or after, until the doctors say it’s safe.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific deterioration triggers and driving advice

SCA_MODELS.text: Right. Okay.
So that I know I’ve explained it properly — what’s going to happen in the next few minutes?
SCA_MODELS.why: Teach-back to confirm he will accept the ambulance

SCA_MODELS.text: You’re ringing the ambulance, I’m not eating or drinking, the wife tells them everything. And I sit tight.
Exactly right. I’ll document all of this and ring your wife later today to check you’ve been seen. Ringing this morning was the right thing to do, Gordon.
SCA_MODELS.why: Documents, closes the loop and follows up

SCA_STEM.name: Gordon Whitfield
pmh: Previous episode of BPPV (years ago, per patient)
SCA_STEM.recent: Telephone call booked this morning: spinning since waking, vomiting. Retired electrician.
SCA_STEM.reason: “The room won’t stop spinning.” Asking for a tablet for vertigo.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG128 (2019, updated 2022) · National Clinical Guideline for Stroke for the UK and Ireland (ICSWP, 2023) · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Constant vertigo with vomiting and inability to walk in a man with vascular risk factors and recent transient focal symptoms is a posterior-circulation stroke until proven otherwise. The action is 999, not a vestibular sedative.

points.t: BPPV causes brief spells of vertigo, lasting seconds, set off by head movement, and the person can usually walk between spells. Constant vertigo for hours, severe vomiting and being unable to stand or walk unaided point to a central cause in the cerebellum or brainstem.

points.h: Look for the company it keeps
points.t: Ask directly about slurred speech, swallowing difficulty, double vision, facial or limb numbness or weakness, clumsiness, and new headache or neck pain (consider vertebral artery dissection). Any one of these with acute vertigo makes a central cause far more likely.

points.h: FAST can miss the back of the brain
points.t: NICE NG128 recommends a validated tool such as FAST outside hospital to screen for stroke, but posterior-circulation strokes often present with vertigo, imbalance and visual symptoms without face, arm or speech signs. A negative FAST does not make this safe.

His two recent episodes of jumbled speech and a clumsy right hand sound like TIAs. NICE NG128: for a suspected TIA with resolved symptoms, give aspirin 300 mg immediately and arrange specialist assessment within 24 hours of onset. That pathway does not apply today, because his symptoms are ongoing.

points.h: Suspected stroke: 999, no aspirin at home
points.t: NICE NG128: aspirin for acute ischaemic stroke is given only after brain imaging has excluded haemorrhage. So with ongoing symptoms, call 999 and do not give aspirin at home. Keep him nil by mouth until a swallow screen has been done.

points.h: Vestibular sedatives mask, they don’t treat
points.t: Prochlorperazine or cyclizine may dampen the vomiting but lose the time window for hyperacute treatment. Prescribing one over the phone with reassurance is the classic error in this presentation.

DVLA: after a TIA or stroke a car driver must stop driving for at least 1 month and may restart only when a clinician says it is safe. Recurrent sudden, disabling dizziness must be reported to the DVLA.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question first; let him give the “ear crystals” story, then agreed to ask specific questions before deciding on treatment.
Retired, lives with his wife; fear of hospital and of being a burden; the wife as a reliable witness and support.
Picked up “the wife made me”, the doorframe, the face “looking off” and the “funny dos”, and explored each.
Idea (old BPPV back), concern (hospital, being a burden, buried fear of mini-strokes), expectation (a tablet, no A&E).
Recognised that a phone call cannot exclude stroke; needs emergency brain imaging. Collateral from his wife in place of an examination.
BPPV vs vestibular neuritis vs posterior-circulation stroke or TIA vs vertebral artery dissection (new neck pain).
Asked about gait, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, numbness, weakness, headache and neck pain; elicited the preceding TIA-like episodes.
Stated suspected posterior-circulation stroke, with recent TIAs, in plain words; did not accept the BPPV label.
999 now; no prochlorperazine; no aspirin before imaging; nil by mouth; stay seated; wife to give the history to the crew.
Linked hypertension, type 2 diabetes and ex-smoking to his stroke risk; secondary prevention left to the stroke team.
Named deterioration triggers, no driving (DVLA), teach-back, documentation and a follow-up call to his wife.

social.t: “At my age” and “not a burden” are common reasons older men delay stroke care. The fear needs naming, not arguing with.
She saw the doorframe and his face. A worried partner is often the most reliable historian in a minimising patient — ask to speak to her, with his agreement.

legal.t: After a TIA or stroke a car driver must stop driving for at least 1 month and restart only when a clinician says it is safe. Recurrent sudden, disabling dizziness must be reported to the DVLA. Tell him not to drive himself to hospital.

If he refused the ambulance, assess his capacity for that decision (Mental Capacity Act 2005). A capacitous refusal must be respected, but explain the risks, keep trying, involve his wife and document carefully.

professional.t: A phone call cannot exclude stroke. When the history points to a central cause, escalate rather than try to examine by phone (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024: recognise the limits of your competence and of the setting).
Record the pattern, the collateral history, the TIA-like episodes, the advice given and the 999 call. Check later that he reached hospital.

community.t: Stroke Association for patients and carers; secondary prevention review in primary care after the stroke team’s plan.

redFlags: Constant vertigo for hours with vomiting and inability to stand or walk unaided
Diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, facial or limb numbness or weakness, clumsiness
New headache or neck pain (possible vertebral artery dissection)
Recent transient speech or limb symptoms (TIAs) and vascular risk factors
psychosocial: Fear of hospital and of being a burden “at my age”
His wife’s alarm as a signal; who is with him now
Driving and practical support for getting to hospital
ice: Concern: hospital, being a burden, and a buried fear that the recent episodes were mini-strokes
Expectation: a tablet for vertigo and no A&E

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Acute constant vertigo with vomiting, gait failure, possible facial asymmetry and new neck pain in a 61-year-old with hypertension, type 2 diabetes and ex-smoking, preceded by two TIA-like episodes: suspected posterior-circulation stroke. Not BPPV.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The ear crystals give short spins when you move your head. What you have is constant, stops you walking, and came after those speech and hand episodes. That can be a stroke at the back of the brain, which often gets mistaken for an ear problem. It needs the stroke team now.”

management.reflectIce: “I can see why the ear crystals feel like the safer answer — and you’ve been wondering if those funny turns were mini-strokes. That’s exactly why we act now.”
management.psychosocial: Enlist his wife, reframe going to hospital as sensible rather than a fuss, and make sure he is not alone or driving.
sharedPlan: 999 now for suspected stroke (NICE NG128); GP makes the call and passes on the history
No vestibular sedative; no aspirin before imaging; nil by mouth until a swallow screen
Stay seated or lying; his wife goes with him and describes the episodes
safetyNet: Worse face, arm, leg or speech, drowsiness or sudden worse headache: ring 999 again
No driving until cleared (DVLA); GP follow-up call later today

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by agreeing with the patient. He brings a ready diagnosis and a simple request; the candidate who tests the pattern, listens to his wife and finds the recent episodes will send him to the stroke team.

items.fail: Prescribing prochlorperazine over the phone because he has had BPPV before.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” BPPV is brief and positional; constant vertigo with gait failure needs emergency assessment.
items.fix: Test the pattern first: “Short bursts when you move your head, or there all the time?” Then: “Can you walk on your own?”

items.fail: Never asking about recent episodes, so the TIAs stay hidden.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” He will not volunteer them.
items.fix: Ask directly: “Any spells recently where your speech or a hand didn’t work properly, even briefly?”

items.fail: Advising aspirin at home while waiting for the ambulance.
items.why: NICE NG128: in suspected acute stroke, aspirin is given only after imaging has excluded haemorrhage.
items.fix: “No aspirin, nothing to eat or drink — they’ll scan you first.”

items.fail: Ignoring the wife in the background, or treating her as interference.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to cues.” Her account (doorframe, face looking off) is the strongest evidence in the call.
items.fix: “Can I speak to your wife for a moment? What have you noticed?”

items.fail: Telling him bluntly “you’re having a stroke, you must go in” without meeting his fear, so he refuses.
items.why: Correct but unpersuasive; a minimising patient who feels bulldozed may decline care.
items.fix: Name the fear he already has about the “funny dos” and use it: “That worry is exactly why we act now.”

items.fail: Closing with “go to A&E if it gets worse”.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and no confirmed plan. He is already an emergency.
items.fix: Make the 999 call yourself or confirm he has, give specific deterioration triggers, check with teach-back and follow up later.
